lead: Expectation is the long-run weighted average of a random variable. Variance measures how far values spread around that average. Together they turn a whole pmf or pdf into two usable numbers. Moments extend the same weighted-sum idea to powers of X, recording shape. Engineers use them to compare noise, signal strength, waiting times and risk. The formulas below cover discrete and continuous variables, the linearity shortcut, and the traps that cost marks.
prereq: You need: Chapter 2.4 for pmf, pdf and CDF, and basic summation and integration.

blocks.text: For a discrete random variable X with pmf p(x)=P(X=x), the expectation is E[X]=Σ x p(x). The sum runs over every value x with p(x)>0. The weights p(x) must sum to 1. For a continuous random variable with pdf f(x), replace the sum by an integral: E[X]=∫ x f(x) dx over the support. The integral must converge absolutely: ∫ |x| f(x) dx < ∞. Absolute convergence stops the answer depending on the order of terms or on cancellation.
E[X] = Σ<sub>x</sub> x p(x) = ∫<sub>−∞</sub><sup>∞</sup> x f(x) dx
blocks.where: p(x) is the discrete pmf; f(x) is the continuous pdf; x is a real value of X.

blocks.text: Expectation is linear. For constants a and b, E[aX+b]=aE[X]+b. For two random variables, E[X+Y]=E[X]+E[Y] when the expectations exist. This holds even if X and Y are dependent. Linearity is why averages are easy to combine.
To average a function g(X), do not transform the mean. Use E[g(X)]=Σ g(x)p(x) for discrete X, or E[g(X)]=∫ g(x)f(x)dx for continuous X. For example, E[X²] weights x² by the same probabilities.

Let μ=E[X]. The variance is Var(X)=E[(X−μ)²]. It is the expected squared distance from the mean. The unit of variance is the square of the unit of X. The standard deviation is σ=√Var(X), in the same unit as X.

blocks.where: μ=E[X]; E[X²]=Σ x² p(x) or ∫ x² f(x)dx; σ=√Var(X).

blocks.text: Use E[X²]−μ² for calculation. Expand the square: E[(X−μ)²]=E[X²−2μX+μ²]=E[X²]−2μE[X]+μ²=E[X²]−μ². The shortcut fails if you subtract in the wrong order.
For constants a and b, Var(aX+b)=a²Var(X). Adding b moves every value but does not change spread. Multiplying by a scales distances by |a|, so squared distances scale by a². In particular, Var(b)=0.

The r-th raw moment is μ′<sub>r</sub>=E[X<sup>r</sup>]. The first raw moment is the mean: μ′<sub>1</sub>=E[X]=μ. The r-th central moment is μ<sub>r</sub>=E[(X−μ)<sup>r</sup>]. The second central moment is the variance: μ<sub>2</sub>=Var(X). The first central moment is always zero, because E[X−μ]=0.

blocks.where: r=1,2,...; μ=E[X]; raw moments are about 0; central moments are about the mean.

blocks.text: Skewness and kurtosis are standardized third and fourth central moments; Unit 1 covers their formulas and interpretation.

For discrete X, μ′<sub>r</sub>=Σ x<sup>r</sup>p(x) and μ<sub>r</sub>=Σ (x−μ)<sup>r</sup>p(x). For continuous X, replace Σ by ∫ and p(x) by f(x). The same absolute-convergence caution applies when r is large.
Conditional expectation E[X|B] uses the conditional pmf or pdf from Chapter 2.2; replace p(x) by p(x|B) or f(x) by f(x|B).

spec.title: Moments for two coin tosses
spec.aria: Table lists x=0,1,2 with probabilities 1/4,1/2,1/4 and weighted products; row sums give E[X]=1 and E[X²]=1.5.

examples.question: X is the number of heads in two fair coin tosses. Find E[X], E[X²] and Var(X).
steps: List the possible values and their probabilities: P(X=0)=1/4, P(X=1)=1/2, P(X=2)=1/4. The probabilities sum to 1.
examples.answer: E[X]=1 head, E[X²]=1.5 heads², and Var(X)=0.5 heads².
examples.check:
xs = [0, 1, 2]
ps = [0.25, 0.5, 0.25]
ex = sum(x * p for x, p in zip(xs, ps))
ex2 = sum((x ** 2) * p for x, p in zip(xs, ps))
var = ex2 - ex ** 2
print(ex)
print(ex2)
print(var)

traps: E[X²] is not (E[X])². For two coin tosses, E[X²]=1.5 but (E[X])²=1.
Var(X) is not E[X²]. You must subtract μ². Reporting 1.5 instead of 0.5 is a common lost mark.
Check that probabilities sum to 1 before using Σx p(x). If they sum to 0.9, the formula gives a weighted total, not an expectation.
Var(aX+b)=a²Var(X), not aVar(X)+b. Adding a constant shifts the mean but does not change spread.
For continuous variables, the expectation integral must converge absolutely. A symmetric-looking integral can hide two divergent tails.

quiz.q: Define E[X] for a discrete random variable.
quiz.a: E[X]=Σ x p(x) over all x with p(x)>0, provided the sum converges absolutely.
Expectation is a weighted average; multiplying every x by a multiplies the weighted sum by a, and adding b adds b times the total weight 1.

quiz.q: X has P(X=−1)=0.2, P(X=0)=0.5, P(X=2)=0.3. Find E[X] and Var(X).
A fair die gives X, the number on the top face. Use E[X] and E[X²] to find Var(X).
If Y=2X+3 and Var(X)=4, find Var(Y) and SD(Y). Explain which quantity changes when 3 is added.
quiz.a: Var(Y)=2²Var(X)=16; SD(Y)=4. Adding 3 shifts the mean by 3 but leaves variance and SD unchanged.

quiz.q: A distribution has μ=10 and E[X²]=125. Find Var(X) and σ. If every value is multiplied by −3, find the new mean, variance and SD.
quiz.a: Var=125−10²=25; σ=5. New mean=−3×10=−30; new variance=(−3)²×25=225; new SD=15.

quiz.q: What is the first central moment and why is it zero?

beyond: Not for the exam. In engineering, expectation and variance are the first two statistics used to model noise, measurement error and signal power. Joint moments become covariance matrices in sensor fusion, Kalman filtering and portfolio risk. Conditional expectation is the base of regression and machine-learning prediction. Search next for law of total expectation, covariance matrix, and moment-based estimators.
